title: 3 tips for choosing your health insurance plan through work
summary: A three-step checklist for choosing an employer health plan: check network providers, consider your care needs and decide how you want to manage costs.

assets.alt: Checklist image of a mother and toddler

atoms.title: Three tips for choosing a plan through work
atoms.question: What are the tips for choosing a health insurance plan through my employer?
atoms.text: At open enrollment, you can use a three-step checklist to weigh the plans your employer offers. 1) Check to see which providers are in network. 2) Consider your health care needs for the year ahead. 3) Decide how you prefer to manage your costs, for example by keeping your monthly premium low or by paying more each month to pay less when you need care.

atoms.title: Check which providers are in network
atoms.question: Why should I check if my providers are in network?
atoms.text: Finding a doctor or clinic that is in network may help keep costs lower, and many plans will only cover network providers. When reviewing plans, check whether your primary doctor, provider or clinic is in network; check whether your mental health providers, dentists and specialty providers are in network; and find out whether there is partial coverage for out-of-network providers.

atoms.title: Using provider search for a UnitedHealthcare plan
atoms.question: How do I find out which doctors are in a UnitedHealthcare network?
atoms.text: If you are considering a UnitedHealthcare plan, you can search for network providers and clinics using the UnitedHealthcare provider search tool. Knowing which providers are in network may help you narrow your health plan choices. For example, if you prefer a specific doctor, you will likely want to be sure that doctor is in network for the plan you choose.

atoms.title: Consider your care needs for the year ahead
atoms.question: How do my health care needs affect which plan I should pick?
atoms.text: Coverage needs may change from year to year, for example because of different medication needs or a procedure planned for the upcoming year. Before you enroll, think about the care you or your family may need in the year ahead. The checklist suggests asking what you see the doctor for, whether you have a major procedure planned, whether you take medications and who else needs coverage through your plan.

atoms.title: Lower premium versus lower copay plans
atoms.question: Should I choose a lower premium plan or a lower copay plan?
atoms.text: Some people prefer to keep their monthly premium low, while others choose to pay higher monthly premiums so they may pay less in copays when they need care. A lower premium plan can save money if you do not have major care needs. A lower copay plan may cost less when you visit a doctor, clinic or urgent care. Compare each plan's deductible, coinsurance and out-of-pocket limit as well.

atoms.title: How a lower premium plan works
atoms.question: What does a lower premium plan mean for my paycheck?
atoms.text: If you do not have any major care needs, you can save money by finding a plan that charges a lower premium each month. This means the plan takes less money out of your paychecks to pay for insurance. Compare your plan options to see which plan's premium amount requires you to pay the least.
questions: How can I pay less each month for health insurance?
Does a lower premium mean less taken from my paycheck?

atoms.title: Compare copays and cost-sharing to avoid surprises
atoms.question: How can I avoid cost surprises with my health plan?
atoms.text: Some plans give you the option to spend less when you pay for care, like visiting the doctor. Consider the cost of copays when you visit a doctor, clinic or urgent care, and compare each plan's deductible, coinsurance and out-of-pocket limit to see which plans may help you save more. Researching these costs and understanding how you and your plan share costs together helps you avoid cost surprises later.
